name: nnotas
tagline: A hosted notes app for capturing, organizing and searching your own written notes.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Notes apps are the most-cloned category in software, and a local one is genuinely a one-sitting build: a text editor, a database, full-text search, tags. What you cannot one-shot is the boring half, meaning sync across devices, a real mobile client, offline conflict resolution and the confidence that your notes will still open in three years. If you live on one machine, the DIY version is not a compromise, it is arguably better because the data is a folder you own. If you capture things on a phone at 2am, you will rebuild half of a sync engine and then quietly go back to paying someone. Details on this specific product are thin, so treat the verdict as a category judgment rather than a feature-by-feature comparison.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that stores markdown notes in SQLite with instant full-text search, tags and one-click export back to plain files.
requirements: A machine you are willing to leave running if you want access from other devices
Optional: a folder in a synced drive if you want crude multi-device support
whatYouLose: Mobile apps, and with them the quick-capture habit that makes notes apps stick
Real sync with conflict handling instead of hoping two devices never edit the same note
Sharing and collaboration on a note with anyone else
Someone else's backups, and someone else's problem when the database file corrupts
Whatever AI, OCR or web-clipper conveniences the hosted product ships
moatNotes: Notes moats are made of accumulated personal content and muscle memory, not technology. Once a few thousand notes live somewhere, the exit cost is emotional as much as technical.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because notes are a habit, and habits break on friction. Paying a few dollars a month means capture works from a phone on a train, search works instantly on every device, and nobody has to think about a database file. A self-hosted clone matches the feature list and loses the reliability, which in this category is most of the product. The people who happily self-host notes are the same people who already enjoy maintaining things; everyone else is buying the absence of maintenance.
notes: The build is easy, the habit is not; judge your clone after two weeks of actual use, not after it renders its first markdown file.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal notes app. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- TypeScript everywhere
- Backend: Node 20 + Fastify
- Database: SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/notes.db
- Frontend: Vite + React, plain CSS, no component library
- Single command dev: npm run dev starts API on 3001 and UI on 5173 with a proxy

Data model:
- notes(id TEXT primary key, title TEXT, body TEXT markdown, created_at, updated_at, archived INTEGER)
- tags(id, name unique), note_tags(note_id, tag_id)
- SQLite FTS5 virtual table over title and body, kept in sync with triggers

Features in scope:
- Two-pane UI: list on the left, editor on the right
- Create, edit, archive, delete notes; autosave 400ms after typing stops
- Markdown editing in a textarea with a live preview toggle, render with marked plus DOMPurify
- Inline #tag parsing from the body, tags become filter chips in the sidebar
- Search box that queries FTS5 as you type, results ranked by bm25, matched terms highlighted
- Keyboard: cmd+k focuses search, cmd+n new note, cmd+enter toggles preview
- Export: POST /api/export writes every note to ./export/YYYY-MM-DD/slug.md with YAML frontmatter for tags and dates
- Import: read any .md files dropped into ./inbox on startup, then move them to ./inbox/processed

Explicitly out of scope: auth, multi-user, sync, mobile app, sharing, AI features, rich text, attachments.

Also deliver: a README with setup in under ten lines, a .env.example with PORT and DB_PATH, and a script npm run backup that copies the db file to ./backups with a timestamp. Seed five example notes on first run so the search is testable immediately.
